topic: Space Hopping: Geometric Interpretation of Non-Square Matrices
target_audience: Undergraduate STEM students or advanced high school students with basic linear algebra knowledge

outline.topic: Space Hopping: Geometric Interpretation of Non-Square Matrices
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate STEM students or advanced high school students with basic linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: Prerequisite Recap: The 'Same-Dimension' Rule
sections.content: Briefly review how square matrices (e.g., 2x2) transform space while staying in the same dimension. Establish the 'Grid' visual: basis vectors i-hat and j-hat moving but remaining on a 2D plane.
sections.example: A 2x2 matrix rotating a 2D drawing of a 'Flatland Cat' 45 degrees while keeping it on the screen.

sections.title: The Tall Matrix: Elevating to 3D (2x3 Transform)
sections.content: Introduce the 3x2 matrix. Explain that it takes 2 input coordinates and outputs 3 coordinates. Geometrically, this maps a 2D plane into a 3D space. The columns represent where the original 2D basis vectors land in the 3D world.
sections.example: A 3x2 matrix lifting a 2D 'Paper Mario' character off a flat page and placing him as a slanted sheet floating in a 3D room.

sections.title: The Wide Matrix: The Great Squish (3x2 Transform)
sections.content: Introduce the 2x3 matrix. This takes a 3D vector and maps it onto a 2D plane. Explain 'Dimensionality Reduction'—how information is lost when we project high-dimensional objects into lower-dimensional spaces.
sections.example: A 3D 'Low-poly Bird' flying in the air, while a 2x3 matrix calculates its 2D shadow cast on the flat ground. The depth information disappears.

sections.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
sections.content: A visual mnemonic for matrix dimensions (m x n). The 'n' (columns) is the dimension of the space we start in (the number of input basis vectors). The 'm' (rows) is the dimension of the space we land in.
sections.example: A 'Magic Portal' analogy: If the portal has 3 input slots but only 2 output wires, the 3D input must be squashed to exit.

sections.title: Column Space: The Footprint of the Transformation
sections.content: Explain that even if a matrix maps to 3D space (3x2), the result is restricted to the span of its columns. This 'Column Space' is the only area in the target dimension that the transformation can reach.
sections.example: A 3x2 matrix creates a 2D 'Glass Pane' floating in a 3D aquarium; the fish (vectors) can only exist on that specific pane, not the whole tank.

sections.title: Summary & Application
sections.content: Synthesize the concept: Non-square matrices are 'Inter-dimensional Bridges.' Mention real-world applications like Computer Vision (projecting 3D scenes onto 2D screens).
sections.example: A camera lens acting as a wide matrix, compressing a 3D mountain range into a 2D digital photo.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Recap: The 'Same-Dimension' Rule
lecture_lines: Square matrices transform space while keeping its dimension.
A 2x2 matrix moves vectors within the 2D plane.
Basis vectors i-hat and j-hat shift but stay flat.
animations: Create a 2D grid with basis vectors i-hat (red #FF0000) and j-hat (green #00FF00) at their standard positions.
Introduce a 2x2 rotation matrix [[cos 45, -sin 45], [sin 45, cos 45]] in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Rotate the entire grid and the 'Flatland Cat' illustration 45 degrees counter-clockwise, keeping the visual strictly 2D.

storyboard.title: The Tall Matrix: Elevating to 3D (2x3 Transform)
lecture_lines: A tall 3x2 matrix maps 2D into 3D space.
Two input coordinates become three output coordinates.
A 2D plane lifts and slants within a 3D room.
animations: Show a 2D plane in a flat perspective with a simple 'Paper Mario' character (#FFFFFF) in the center.
Display a 3x2 matrix on the left side with columns highlighted in cyan (#00FFFF) to represent new basis vectors.
Rotate the camera to a 3D perspective as the 2D plane lifts and transforms into a slanted sheet (#FFFF00) floating in 3D space.

storyboard.title: The Wide Matrix: The Great Squish (3x2 Transform)
lecture_lines: A wide 2x3 matrix squashes 3D into 2D space.
Three input coordinates are projected onto a flat plane.
Depth information disappears during this dimensional reduction.
animations: Display a 3D coordinate system containing a white (#FFFFFF) low-poly bird model flying above a flat ground.
Introduce a 2x3 projection matrix in magenta (#FF00FF) that maps 3D coordinates to the 2D ground plane.
Project a grey (#808080) shadow of the bird onto the ground plane, showing how the bird's height is lost in the 2D shadow.

storyboard.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
lecture_lines: Matrix dimensions m-by-n describe the transformation's path.
The column count n is the starting space dimension.
The row count m is the target space dimension.
animations: Write the dimensions 'm x n' where 'n' (columns) is blue (#0000FF) and 'm' (rows) is red (#FF0000).
Animate a 'Magic Portal' with 3 input slots (blue #0000FF) and 2 output paths (red #FF0000) to represent a 2x3 transformation.
Briefly flash the input vectors entering the slots and the resulting smaller-dimension vectors exiting the paths.

storyboard.title: Column Space: The Footprint of the Transformation
lecture_lines: Outputs are restricted to the span of the columns.
This reachable region is called the Column Space.
A 3x2 matrix fills a 2D pane in 3D.
animations: Render a 3D wireframe cube (#FFFFFF) to represent the target 3D space of a 3x2 transformation.
Draw two basis vectors in the cube (#00FF00 and #FF00FF) starting from the origin.
Create a semi-transparent 2D plane (Column Space) that spans these two vectors, showing it is the only reachable area in the tank.

storyboard.title: Summary & Application
lecture_lines: Non-square matrices act as bridges between different dimensions.
Cameras project 3D worlds onto 2D digital sensors.
Linear algebra powers these inter-dimensional transformations.
animations: Show icons of various non-square matrices acting as bridges between different sized grids.
Visualize a 3D mountain range scene (#00FF00) that passes through a 'camera lens' matrix.
Display the final 2D digital photograph on a flat screen (#FFFFFF), illustrating the projection from 3D to 2D.
